title: 1948: Programs become data
text: You begin where software began: a computer that keeps its instructions in memory beside its data. Changing the program now means changing numbers, not rewiring a machine.

title: 1949: Names for numbers
text: Programmers stop writing raw binary. Short names for instructions, translated by a program, are the first step in a long line of tools that write code for you.

title: 1957: The compiler wins
text: FORTRAN shows that a compiler can match hand-written machine code. After this, programmers describe what they want and let the machine work out how.

title: 1968: A crisis gets a name
text: Big projects run late and break. A NATO meeting calls the problem "software engineering", and the rest of this map is a search for what actually helps.

title: 1972: C and Unix
text: Dennis Ritchie's small, fast language and the operating system written in it become the template for nearly everything that follows, including Linux today.

title: 1974: Ask for what you want
text: Databases get a question language. You describe the answer you need and the system plans how to fetch it. Fifty years on, SQL is still the default.

title: 1975: The mythical man-month
text: Fred Brooks, drawing on IBM's System/360 project, reports that adding people to a late project makes it later. Many of today's arguments about process start here.

title: 1983: Objects go mainstream
text: C++ adds classes to C, and object-oriented programming spreads from research labs into everyday work.

title: 1991: The web arrives
text: A hypertext system from CERN becomes the default place for software to live. In the same year a student announces a free Unix-like kernel called Linux.

title: 1995: JavaScript
text: Within weeks in May 1995, Brendan Eich builds the first prototype of a scripting language that ends up in every browser. It outgrows its origins and, with Node.js, escapes the browser entirely.

title: 2001: Agile
text: Seventeen developers meet in Utah and write a manifesto for short iterations and working software. Whether teams do it well is another matter.

title: 2005: Git
text: After the Linux kernel loses its BitKeeper license, Linus Torvalds starts writing a distributed version control system. It becomes the universal way to share and merge code.

title: 2006: The cloud
text: Amazon starts renting servers by the hour. Containers and Kubernetes follow, and infrastructure becomes something you write as code.

title: Other people's code
text: One command now pulls in hundreds of libraries. It is the magic of modern programming and its biggest risk.

title: Machines that check machines
text: Linters, type checkers, tests and continuous integration review every change before a person sees it. A 1978 tool called lint started the line.

title: 2016: Eleven lines break the web
text: A tiny deleted package breaks thousands of builds. The lesson about fragile dependency chains is sharpened by later attacks.

title: Now: code written with AI
text: Language models write, review and repair code. The evidence on how much they help is mixed and still being gathered. You wake up in the middle of that change.
